newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Meningitis killed 16,000 in 1996 and spreading-WHO.
newsitem.headline: Meningitis killed 16,000 in 1996 and spreading-WHO.

text.p: The World Health Organisation reported on Wednesday an alarming increase in meningitis epidemics in Africa and called for immediate vaccination campaigns to stop the spread of the life-threatening disease.

The United Nations health agency said that meningitis killed 16,000 people, mostly children, in Africa in 1996, the highest number of victims in one year, out of a total of around 150,000 reported cases.

WHO said sub-Saharan Africa anticipated another wave of severe meningitis outbreaks in 1997 and it launched an emergency appeal for $6.3 million to purchase and distribute meningitis vaccine which costs 18 cents a dose.

David Heymann, WHO's head of emerging and other communicable diseases control, said mass movements of refugee populations in Africa and the expansion in dry zones because of climate changes were the main reasons behind the disease's spread.
"1996 was the worst year in terms of victims on record," he told a news conference.

Heymann said scientists had no clear idea about the process that turns harmless bacteria into potential killers. Meningitis, an inflammation of the brain and spinal cord, has two main forms -- bacterial and viral and the former is more dangerous.
Heymann said two people in ten harmlessly carry the bacteria which produce meningococcal infection in their noses and throats.
Mass vaccination with antibiotics could prevent deaths at an earlier stage, he said.
The WHO said it will receive 14 million doses of meningitis vaccine from producers in 1997 to control the epidemic.
Heymann said the "meningitis belt" in Africa, stretching from Senegal to Ethiopia, was spreading farther south in the absence of monitoring and vaccination campaigns.
"The poor countries in Africa which are unable to mobilise funds for vaccines suffer," Heymann said. "In 1997, the countries of sub-Saharan Africa anticipate another wave of serious outbreaks."
In Europe, up to 5,000 cases were reported in 1996, including between 400 and 700 in France, Heymann said.
Fatality rates were less than one percent when the disease was properly treated.
The epidemic has already begun this year in the West African country of Togo, where it killed at least 136 people from 929 reported cases, WHO said.

Meninigitis torments arid regions of West Africa during the dry season. An epidemic which swept Sahelian West Africa for months from February last year killed hundreds of people in northern Nigeria, Niger, Burkina Faso and Mali.
